title: The Engraved Heart, the Tree by the Water, and the Sabbath
summary: Judah's sin is engraved on the people's hearts and on their altars, and it will cost them their land. Two paths are set side by side: the one who trusts in human strength is like a desert shrub, while the one who trusts the LORD is like a tree by the stream. The chapter confesses that the heart is deceitful and that only God searches it, gives Jeremiah's third confession, and ends with a call to keep the Sabbath holy at the gates of Jerusalem.
story: Chapters 11 to 20 alternate between judgment on Judah and the prophet's personal laments, and chapter 17 contains both, along with wisdom sayings and a sermon on the Sabbath. It is a collection rather than a single speech, but a thread runs through it: the heart. Sin is carved into it (verse 1), trust turns it toward or away from God (verse 5), it is deceitful beyond cure (verse 9), and God alone searches it (verse 10). The chapter explains why outward reforms keep failing in Judah, and it prepares for the promise of chapter 31, where God will write his law on the heart instead.
historical:
The chapter contains no date. Verses 1 to 4 fit the late years of the kingdom, when the worship at local shrines that Josiah had tried to stamp out in the 620s BC had revived. Verses 3 and 4 repeat, with small differences, the threat of 15:13-14. The “Asherah poles” of verse 2 were wooden cult objects associated with the goddess Asherah, a major deity of the Canaanite world. Inscriptions found at Kuntillet Ajrud in the Sinai and at Khirbet el-Qom near Hebron, dated to around the eighth century BC, speak of blessing by the LORD and his asherah, evidence that some Israelites paired the worship of Israel's God with this goddess or her symbol, which is exactly the mixture the prophets condemned.

The Sabbath sermon in verses 19 to 27 names “the gate of the people” as the gate through which the kings go in and out; its location is unknown. The concern it addresses, trade carried on through the city gates on the Sabbath, appears again after the exile, when Nehemiah shut Jerusalem's gates on the Sabbath to stop merchants from bringing in goods (Nehemiah 13:15-22). Some scholars think this passage was shaped by that later concern; others see no reason it could not come from Jeremiah's own time, since Sabbath-breaking is also condemned in earlier prophets (Amos 8:5).
cultural:
An “iron stylus” with “a diamond point” was a tool for cutting inscriptions into stone or metal, writing meant to last. The “horns” of the altar were projections at its four corners; on the Day of Atonement and in sin offerings the priest smeared blood on them for cleansing (Leviticus 4:7; 16:18). Jeremiah says Judah's sin is written in the very place meant for its removal. The “green trees” and “high hills” were the traditional sites of local shrines, which the prophets and the book of Kings repeatedly condemn.

The proverb of the partridge (verse 11) seems to draw on a popular belief that this bird hatched eggs it had not laid, only to have the chicks leave it once grown. Ill-gotten wealth is like that: it does not stay. The Sabbath was the seventh day of rest commanded in the Ten Commandments, a sign of the covenant (Exodus 31:13) and a weekly reminder that Israel's life depended on God, not on endless work. Carrying loads through the gates on the Sabbath meant doing market business as on any other day. The offerings listed in verse 26 (burnt offerings, sacrifices, grain offerings, frankincense, and thank offerings) cover the whole range of temple worship, from the regions around Jerusalem: Benjamin, the foothills (the Shephelah), the hill country, and the Negev in the south.
literary: The chapter is a collection of units. Verses 1 to 4 are a prose-poetic oracle of judgment. Verses 5 to 8 are a wisdom poem on two ways, built on a curse and a blessing, very close in form and imagery to Psalm 1: a dry shrub and a fruitful tree. Verses 9 to 11 add two wisdom sayings, one on the heart and one on unjust wealth. Verses 12 and 13 are a short hymn, and verses 14 to 18 are the third of Jeremiah's confessions, a lament asking for healing and vindication. Verses 19 to 27 are a prose sermon with a conditional structure typical of Jeremiah's prose: if you listen, the city will stand; if you do not, it will burn. The recurring word “heart” ties the first half together, and the recurring images of water and drought (the desert, the stream, the fountain of living water) join the wisdom poem to the hymn.

outline.t: Sin engraved on the heart and the altar
The shrub in the desert and the tree by the stream
The deceitful heart and the unjust fortune
The glorious throne and the fountain of living water
Jeremiah's confession: heal me, and I will be healed

doctrines.note: The chapter locates sin in the heart, not only in acts: it is engraved there, and the heart itself is “deceitful above all things and beyond cure”. Self-knowledge alone cannot fix it, since the instrument of self-examination is the thing that is damaged.
Verses 5 to 8 make trust the dividing line between life and barrenness. Faith is not a feeling but where a person sends their roots: toward human strength or toward the LORD.
The Sabbath command is presented as a test of whether Judah will listen. Keeping it was an act of trust that God, not ceaseless trade, sustained the city.
“Heal me, O LORD, and I will be healed” teaches that healing and salvation are God's to give. Jeremiah's prayer holds trust and complaint together.

words.note: Aqov, deceitful, crooked, or insidious (verse 9). The word comes from the same root as the name Jacob (Ya'aqov), the patriarch who deceived his brother and father, and many interpreters hear a deliberate echo: the heart of every child of Jacob carries Jacob's old crookedness. The root has to do with the heel, and with tripping up or supplanting.

Batach, to trust, rely on, or feel secure in. It appears in both halves of the wisdom poem: cursed is the one who trusts in mankind, blessed is the one who trusts in the LORD. In Jeremiah the word often exposes false securities, such as the temple (7:4) and fortified cities (5:17). The question is never whether we trust but in what.

Shabbat, the Sabbath, from a verb meaning to cease or stop. It occurs seven times in verses 21 to 27. For Israel it was a weekly day of rest, rooted both in creation (Exodus 20:11) and in the rescue from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15). To keep it was to confess that a people who had once been slaves now belonged to a God who gives rest.

christ: The chapter's diagnosis of the heart sets up the promise of 31:33, where God will write his law on hearts instead of stone, a promise the New Testament says is fulfilled in the new covenant Christ established (Hebrews 8:10). Jesus himself is described in John's Gospel as knowing what is in every person (John 2:24-25), and in Revelation the risen Christ speaks in the language of verse 10 when he says he searches minds and hearts and repays each according to their deeds (Revelation 2:23). The God whom verse 13 calls “the fountain of living water” is echoed when Jesus offers living water to a Samaritan woman and to the crowds at a festival (John 4:10-14; 7:37-38). And the Sabbath, a sign of rest, points toward the rest Jesus offers to the weary (Matthew 11:28) and which Hebrews 4 describes as still remaining for God's people.

hard.q: Does this chapter make the whole city's fate depend on a rule about carrying loads, and how should Christians read the Sabbath command today?
hard.a: Verses 24 to 27 can sound as though Jerusalem's survival hangs on a single regulation. But in Jeremiah the Sabbath functions as a test case for the whole covenant: whether the people would stop, listen, and trust God rather than their own work and trade. The prophets never treat Sabbath-keeping as a substitute for justice or faithfulness; they treat its neglect as a symptom of a heart that has stopped listening. How Christians apply the command is a second-order question on which faithful traditions differ. Some hold that the Sabbath principle carries over to the Lord's Day, Sunday, as a day of worship and rest. Others, including Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists, keep the seventh day itself. Others read the New Testament (Colossians 2:16-17; Hebrews 4) as saying the Sabbath is fulfilled in the rest Christ gives, leaving the observance of days to conscience (Romans 14:5-6). All agree that the command's heart, rest received as a gift and trust in God over ceaseless striving, still speaks.

questions: Where are your roots? What do you instinctively trust when a year of drought comes: your own strength, other people, or God?
If the heart is deceitful beyond our understanding, how can a person know themselves truly? What role do God, Scripture, and other people play?
What would it look like to practice rest as an act of trust, and what does your resistance to rest reveal?
